name: Tomas Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play trumpet in a theatre brass section, record short entry cues and teach two teenagers after school. My music degree and twenty-five years of paid shows help me hear a late attack; I still wipe the valves myself before every call. I enjoy the first clean blast when the whole section lands together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do those calls fit your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner has steady hours at a grocery store and our children are grown. We rent and have three months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for a working player, with some other theatres nearby, but a spare chair is not a posted job. I use AI now and then for a draft set list, then check it against the stage manager's signed page.

say: I'd accept **faster set lists** with paid rehearsal and show times intact.
I'd say a **trumpet entrance** still follows an actor's breath.
think: Our **three-month reserve** and partner wage cover one delayed fee.
A **written cancellation term** matters after a moved spring show.
do: Confirm **seven paid calls** and two pupil slots; request written cancellation pay this week.
Check **AI set lists** against signed pages and save one quarter of extra cleared wedding fees after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** while paid calls and household wages hold.
S0.quote: The trumpet still has to meet the actor's breath.
fieldNote: His **typical pay** and three-month reserve absorb one moved show while his partner earns steady wages.
His occasional **AI set-list drafts** are checked against signed pages and use no cast audio.

steps.text: Confirm seven paid theatre calls and two pupils; request written cancellation fee
Check AI lists against signed page; save quarter of extra cleared wedding after rent/food/repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the section that a faster set list is fine if our paid rehearsal and show times remain on it. The trumpet still has to meet the actor's breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months saved and my partner's steady grocery wage let us absorb one delayed fee. I still want a written cancellation term after a spring show moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm seven paid theatre calls and two pupil slots, and request a written cancellation fee. In the first year of this mild change I'll keep checking occasional AI set-list drafts against the signed page and save a quarter of each extra cleared wedding set after rent, food and trumpet repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the booked work. A moved show would be irritating, but we could still pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the spring show moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lighting fault moved the spring show by five weeks. We were paid the rehearsal but had no written rule for the lost performance night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes into your draft set list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't give an AI list a cast recording. Titles and times are enough, and I check them before anyone gets a notice.

say: I'd ask which **paid entry cues** software would replace.
I'd seek **written fees** for live playing and revisions before another season.
think: Entry cues bring **one fifth** of my own pay.
Our **three-month reserve** gives time to respond, not permanent replacement income.
do: Count **ten cue invoices** and request a paid engineer demonstration outside booked shows.
Test **AI timing checker** after paid demo on owned nameless audio, theatre-funded paid-use licence and approved local storage.
Compare **each cue by ear**; stop altered notes or leaks and require written learner permission for other audio.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic cut to cue fees.
S1.quote: A quicker edit is useful, but it will not make the theatre buy a recording.
fieldNote: The **new checker** requires paid instruction outside show hours and a theatre-funded licence permitting paid use.
The **test cue** is owned, nameless and locally stored, with ear checks and stop rules.

steps.text: Count ten cue invoices and request paid engineer demo outside booked shows
Test after paid demo: owned nameless cue, theatre-funded paid-use licence and approved local storage
Listen against original; stop altered notes or leaks; require learner permission for other audio

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the theatre which paid trumpet entry cues its software will replace. I would ask for written live and revision fees before agreeing to another season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The short cues bring about one fifth of my own pay. A smaller order book would hurt, though three months saved and my partner's wage give us time to find a response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll count my last ten cue invoices and ask the house engineer for a paid demonstration of a new AI timing checker. In the first year I'll test only a nameless cue I own if the theatre pays for a licence allowing paid use and approved local storage; I'll listen against the original, stop for altered notes or a file leaving the theatre, and keep my paid calls rather than replace one with training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the cue fees shrinking. A quicker edit is useful, but it will not make the theatre buy a recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the timing-checker lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The engineer must show it on a paid hour outside my booked show. If the lesson takes a paid call or I must buy the licence, I'll use the old recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use a student's recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't upload either teenager's playing. A student's recording would need written family permission and an approved storage rule first.

say: I'd warn **2028 thinking AGI** reaches cues before 2031 trumpet-playing robots.
I'd ask for **signed live calls** while the theatre still books us.
think: I expect **one-fifth pay** from cue orders to end in 2028.
Further **live-show cuts** remain possible, not my forecast.
do: Total **cue income**, request signed theatre dates and actual pension estimate before stopping paid work.
Seek **posted brass-tutor work** after live cuts only if degree/teaching qualify, written net after travel replaces losses and late bus runs.
Keep **theatre calls and pupils** until a suitable signed offer arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected cue loss with a search window.
S2.quote: Three months saved do not pay years of rent.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 cue loss** comes before 2031 playing robots; live cuts remain conditional.
A school move needs **posted qualification**, written replacement net after travel, late-bus access and signed offer.

steps.text: Total cue income; request signed paid theatre dates and actual pension estimate
Seek posted school brass-tutor job after live cuts if music degree/teaching qualify and bus runs
Require written net after travel replacing losses; keep theatre/pupils until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the brass section that thinking AGI by 2028 can make entry cues before any robot can play trumpet. Playing robots follow around 2031, so I would ask for signed live calls now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect cue orders to end in 2028 and take one fifth of my pay. Live shows may also thin later, but the seven dates I can see have not been cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total cue pay, ask for signed paid theatre dates and request an actual pension estimate before talking about stopping at 60. In the first year after 2028, if paid live shows also fall, I'll seek a posted school brass-tutor role only if my music degree and teaching history qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the late bus runs; I'll keep theatre calls and pupils until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a regular fifth of my income. Three months saved and some nearby employers give me search time; a live-show collapse would be a worse, conditional blow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a school tutor job available now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is no school offer today. I will read a current paid posting and its qualifications before I count a tutor wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop playing at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need an actual pension figure before changing paid work. Three months saved do not pay years of rent.

say: I'd seek **paid brass repair learning** during the five-year warning.
I'd note **2034 playing robots** follow earlier recording changes.
think: I need **recognized, supervised training** before shop chemicals or metal repair.
do: Take **recognised repair training** only with funded paid place, matched displaced show wages, preserved pupil lessons, safety gear and qualified supervision.
Seek **posted repair work** after both 2031 cue/show cuts if certificate qualifies; written replacement net after travel, buses fit.
Keep **paid theatre/pupils** until signed offer; use tools/chemicals under qualified lead until safety sign-off.
feel: I feel **anxious** until paid training and a real job exist.
S3.quote: A brass-repair certificate local employers reject would be six months away from paid music for no gain.
fieldNote: The **six-month training** needs employer recognition before enrolment, funded tuition, actual paid place and protected theatre wages.
The **repair work** requires safety gear, a qualified lead, signed checks, posted paid work and replacement net after travel.

steps.text: Confirm certificate recognition before funded paid training; protect show wages/pupil slots; require safety gear/qualified supervision
Work under qualified repair lead with safety gear until tool/chemical checks are signed
Seek certificate-qualified posted repair job after both cue/show cuts, with buses fitting shifts
Require written net after travel replacing losses; keep paid theatre/pupils until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre that five years to AGI by 2031 could let me learn paid brass-instrument repair. Playing robots follow around 2034, after software has already changed recording work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cues could lose their buyers before 2031 under ordinary software. I know how to clean a valve, but I have not been trained to fix a dent or handle shop chemicals alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll ask the repair shop which local employers recognize its six-month brass-repair certificate before enrolling. I'll take an actual paid workshop place only if the shop funds tuition and supplies safety gear, wages match any paid theatre calls its hours displace, my paid pupil slots remain intact, and a qualified repair lead supervises tool and chemical work. In the first year after 2031, if cues end and paid shows also fall, I'll seek a posted paid repair-assistant role only if the certificate qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses run after shifts; I'll keep theatre and pupil work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious until the place and the job both pay. A brass-repair certificate local employers reject would be six months away from paid music for no gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you handle repairs alone after training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not use solvents or straighten metal alone after a course. A qualified lead must check the first repairs and sign the safety sheet before I work independently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if tuition is funded but wages are lower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop covers fees but pays less than my lost show hours, I'll wait for another intake. A free course can still cost us rent.

say: I'd check **actual retirement pay** during the decade before 2036.
I'd say **2039 trumpet robots** do not remove today's rent bill.
think: At **68**, I may still need theatre and pupil pay.
Our **three-month reserve** and unknown pension do not fund retirement.
do: Request **actual pension statements** and two-year paid theatre plan; keep booked shows/pupils until signed offer.
Save **one quarter** of extra cleared festival fees after rent, food and repairs toward five months.
Seek **degree/teaching-qualified tutor job** after 2036 live cuts and pension gap; posted pay, written replacement net after travel, bus fits.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant pay while current bookings hold.
S4.quote: I will not put an invented pension amount into our rent plan.
fieldNote: His **five-month savings goal** uses a quarter of genuine extra cleared festival pay after essentials.
A **school tutor move** needs a real paid posting, degree/teaching fit, written replacement net, bus and signed offer.

steps.text: Request actual pension statements and written two-year theatre call plan
Save 25% of extra cleared festival fees after rent/food/trumpet repairs toward five months
Keep paid shows/pupils after 2036 until suitable signed offer
Seek degree/teaching-qualified posted tutor after live cuts and pension gap; written replacement net after travel, bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 is time to learn what retirement really pays. Trumpet-playing robots follow around 2039, but a birthday does not pay our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still want and need paid theatre and pupil work. Three months saved now and an unknown pension cannot tell us when I can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year theatre call plan, then save a quarter of each extra cleared festival set after rent, food and trumpet repairs toward five months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid shows and pupils while booked; if live pay falls and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted school brass-tutor job only if my degree and teaching experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the late bus works, keeping current work until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant bookings, though paid calls and three months saved give us room to check. I will not put an invented pension amount into our rent plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra festival set pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there is no extra festival set, I save nothing from it. I won't move grocery money just to reach five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen a pension statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't seen a pension statement yet. I will check it against our bills and actual paid calls before cutting a single show.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue fees could stop before I find another paid role. Signed theatre dates, actual pension figures and a posted qualifying tutor job with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first brass repair after a course. A workshop certificate cannot hold a trumpet valve steady for me.

headlineQuote: A workshop certificate cannot hold a trumpet valve steady for me.
portrait: Tomas is a **58-year-old experienced trumpeter** with a music degree, partner and grown children.
His **typical pay**, three-month reserve and some nearby theatres give a limited search window if cues end.
He uses **AI occasionally** for set lists and learns a new timing checker only with paid instruction and safe owned audio.
He explores **paid brass repair training** only with recognized qualification, protected wages, funded gear and supervised work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a fifth of Tomas's income from recorded cues.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre dates**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying work with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
